summary: Arabic marks a definite noun with the prefix al- (الْ), written joined to the noun, and an indefinite noun with nunation (tanwīn: -un, -an, -in). There is no word for “a”: بَيْتٌ = a house, الْبَيْتُ = the house. Before the 14 sun letters (ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن) the l of al- is assimilated: it carries no sukūn and the next letter gets a šadda — الشَّقَّةُ = aš-šaqqa. Diptotes (نَوَافِذُ، مَصَابِيحُ، طَمَاطِم) never take tanwīn, and indeclinable words in -ā / -ī (كُوسَا، بْرُوكُلِي) show definiteness only by al-. General statements (“I like tomatoes”) use al-: أُحِبُّ الطَّمَاطِمَ.

askYourself: Is the noun specific (one we both know) or meant in general (“books”, “onions as food”)? → al-
Is it one of many, not identified (“a book”)? → tanwīn, no al-
Does the noun start with a sun letter? → no sukūn on the l, šadda on the letter (الشَّقَّةُ)
Is the noun a diptote or indeclinable? → no tanwīn even when it is indefinite
Is my indefinite noun the subject? → put the place first: هُنَا كِتَابٌ
After adding al-, did I remove the tanwīn?
steps: Choose the case ending (-u nominative, -a accusative, -i genitive).
Write al- (sun or moon letter rule) or the tanwīn form.

traps: Generic = definite: هِيَ تُحِبُّ الْخِيَارَ = she likes cucumbers (in general), not only “the cucumbers”.
هٰذِهِ جَزَرَةٌ (“this is a carrot” — a sentence) vs هٰذِهِ الْجَزَرَةُ (“this carrot” — a phrase): the article changes the structure.
What you have with عِنْدَ is indefinite and nominative: عِنْدِي جَزَرَةٌ.
With a sun letter you hear no l: الطَّمَاطِمُ = aṭ-ṭamāṭimu.
*كِتَابٌ هُنَا → هُنَا كِتَابٌ (an indefinite subject follows the place).

definite (the …) — al-

blocks.title: General = definite.
blocks.text: الْكُتُبُ مُفِيدَةٌ = books are useful (in general); أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ = I like coffee. English and German leave the article out here; Arabic, like Greek, puts it in.

blocks.title: An indefinite subject goes after the place.
blocks.text: “A book is here” is not *كِتَابٌ هُنَا: say هُنَا كِتَابٌ (there is a book here). With the article the order is the other way: الْكِتَابُ هُنَا (the book is here).
With a demonstrative the article turns a sentence into a phrase: هٰذَا كِتَابٌ = this is a book; هٰذَا الْكِتَابُ = this book.

quiz.why: ش is a sun letter: the l assimilates; and al- and tanwīn never go together.

quiz.q: Which noun starts with a sun letter?
quiz.why: س is a sun letter: السَّرِيرُ; ب, ك, ق are moon letters.
An indefinite subject follows the place; الْقَلَمُ هُنَا = the pen is here.

quiz.q: Can a noun have al- and tanwīn at the same time?
quiz.why: Definite = al-, indefinite = tanwīn: *الْبَيْتٌ is impossible.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew הַ־ is a prefix too and Hebrew has no “a” either; instead of sun letters, הַ doubles the next consonant with a dagesh (הַבַּיִת), and there is no tanwīn.
German has two articles, der / die / das and ein / eine, and both change for case; Arabic folds “the” and “a” into the noun.
Chinese has no articles: 书 is “a book” or “the book” from the context; 这本书 = this book.
هٰذَا كِتَابٌ (this is a book) vs هٰذَا الْكِتَابُ (this book): the article decides.
